children: Investors captivated by artificial intelligence’s earnings potential may be overlooking the growing threat of tightening liquidity to the stock market, Société Générale strategist Albert Edwards warned.

In his Nov. 12 report, the lead analyst said dwindling financial support for risk assets, fading momentum in earnings upgrades and renewed inflation pressure threaten to destabilize the equity rally. His analysis challenged the belief that strong corporate profit forecasts would be sufficient to keep technology shares climbing.

image.alt: Simon White of Bloomberg published this chart a few days before the mid-term elections, according to Societe Generale.

children: Edwards questioned why explanations of the technology selloff following the U.S. midterm elections had paid so little attention to liquidity. He cited Bloomberg strategist Simon White’s research tracking money-supply growth relative to nominal economic growth as an indication of whether sufficient funds were available to support asset prices. Edwards argued that commentators frequently constructed economic explanations after markets had already moved, overlooking changes in the money supporting those markets.
“A macro narrative is often invented by us legions of commentators, after the event,” he wrote.

That concern carried particular significance for semiconductor investors. Edwards highlighted White’s analysis identifying chips as the sector most positively sensitive to the yield curve over the horizon examined, followed by energy. The liquidity squeeze therefore threatened an AI trade that had already encountered questions about enormous capital expenditures and potential excess computing capacity. For investors who had treated the industry’s spending boom as evidence of durable demand, the report raised the possibility that financing conditions could overwhelm otherwise persuasive growth narratives.
Earnings trends supplied another warning. Forecast profit growth for U.S. technology companies and the S&P 500 (

) remained strong, but Edwards noted that the breadth of analysts’ earnings upgrades had started to deteriorate. The pace of improvement in technology earnings revisions had also turned downward, a development he presented as a potential leading signal for equities. His point was that investors needed to examine whether expectations were still improving, even when the headline growth figures remained impressive.

Edwards had established his reputation as a perma-bear in 1996 with his Ice Age thesis, which argued that deflation would cause stocks to collapse and bond values to climb. His latest report, however, also described a threat from the opposite direction: inflation that could force interest rates higher. That concern complicated the investment outlook because renewed monetary tightening could place additional pressure on equities already struggling with reduced liquidity and less favorable earnings revisions.

Annual inflation readings had offered some reassurance. Edwards noted that core consumer inflation excluding shelter had hovered around 2% for roughly three years, supporting his previously sanguine assessment. More recent three-month annualized measures had become less comfortable, however, including a measure excluding both shelter and used cars. He warned that another monthly increase of 0.3% would deepen the problem, suggesting that apparently benign annual figures could obscure a meaningful acceleration beneath the surface.

Corporate pricing data reinforced his unease. Edwards said the third-quarter productivity report had confirmed that the second-quarter jump in corporate output-price inflation above 4% had not been a one-off. Sharp increases in that series had historically tended to accompany stronger core consumer inflation, he argued.
“I for one am concerned,” he wrote.
He raised the prospect of Federal Reserve rate increases exceeding 200 basis points, or two percentage points, although he didn't provide a formal forecast or timetable.

For investors, Edwards’s message was that enthusiasm about AI profits needed to be weighed against the financial conditions supporting share prices. His report directed attention toward liquidity, the momentum of earnings revisions and shorter-term inflation measures. Together, those indicators suggested that strong growth stories could still face substantial market pressure if money became scarcer and the prospect of higher interest rates returned.

title: SocGen's Albert Edwards warns liquidity squeeze, inflation threaten AI stock rally
